summary_html: Reports via **state hotlines** (anonymous or confidential). CAPTA conditions funding on operating intake systems with confidentiality and good-faith protections.
authority_html: - **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — intake, confidentiality, immunity, and data requirements tied to federal funding

primary_citations.citation_text: District of Columbia - D.C. Code Title 4, Chapter 13 (Child Abuse and Neglect)
District of Columbia - D.C. Code § 4-1321.02 (Mandatory reporters)
District of Columbia - D.C. Code § 22-3020.52 (Reporting requirements and privileges — child sexual abuse)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: D.C. Code § 4-1321.04 confers on good-faith mandatory reporters immunity from liability rather than immunity from suit, so the denial of that immunity is not effectively unreviewable after final judgment and cannot be appealed under the collateral order doctrine; the interlocutory appeal was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
key_cases.relevance: It explains the statutory presumption of good faith that protects hotline reporters from suit for damages.
key_cases.quote: mandatory reporters are shielded from liability, both civil and criminal, for reports made in good faith, even if those reports ultimately turn out to be mistaken

key_cases.court: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
key_cases.holding: When CPS receives a report identifying particular children as abused, the Child Abuse Prevention Act creates a special relationship imposing on the District a duty to take the steps the Act prescribes for those children, so summary judgment for the District was error.
key_cases.relevance: It makes a hotline report the trigger that converts the District's general public duty into a special duty to the named children.
key_cases.quote: From that moment on, the District had a duty to take certain steps prescribed by the Act for the protection of those children.

mandatory_reporters: Employee, agent, or contractor of the Child and Family Services Agency — D.C. Code § 4-1321.02(a)
Individual involved in the care and treatment of patients
Humane officer of any agency charged with the enforcement of animal cruelty laws
Employee of the Department of Parks and Recreation
Any person 18 or older, for suspected sexual abuse of a child under 16 — D.C. Code § 22-3020.52(a)
reporting_details: The District is not a universal-reporter jurisdiction: D.C. Code § 4-1321.02(a) names 19 categories of mandatory reporter, who report abuse, neglect, sexual abuse, or a non-accidental bullet, knife, or sharp-object injury to CFSA or the Metropolitan Police Department under § 4-1321.02(b)(1)(A), (C), and (D), but must report to CFSA alone when a child aged 5 through 13 has 10 or more days of unexcused absences within a school year — § 4-1321.02(b)(1)(B), the District's truancy trigger. D.C. Code § 22-3020.52(a) separately requires any person 18 or older to report suspected sexual abuse of a child under 16 (both terms defined in § 22-3020.51), a call to 911 or a report to CFSA counting as a report to the police.
